item.title: Why Sleep Matters for Brain Inflammation
item.description:
Traumatic Brain Injury

Why Sleep Matters for Brain Inflammation

Sleep can help improve neurological ill health, including encephalitis.

Posted July 28, 2026

Key points
  • Quality sleep is essential for brain recovery and immune system regulation.
  • Many health conditions including encephalitis can be improved with better sleep.
  • Family members, caregivers, and patient organizations can play a crucial role in supporting healthy sleep.

By Prav Prathapan

“Sleep’s the only medicine that gives ease.”—Sophocles.

Sleep is something most of us take for granted. However, increasing research indicates that it significantly improves a range of conditions. Whilst many people may understand that sleep can broadly improve mood and stress, it is increasingly understood that ‘sleep hygiene’ can significantly address brain health.

Source: Stock-Asso Adobe Stock

Sleeping for Brain Recovery

Sleep is not merely rest. It is an active and essential process during which the brain repairs itself. During non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep, the brain’s energy expenditure is about 85 percent of waking levels (1). The brain clears out metabolic waste products via the newly discovered glymphatic system and reinforces neural connections (2). For someone recovering from encephalitis (brain inflammation), for example, where inflammation might have damaged brain tissue and disrupted neural networks, this maintenance becomes critical. NREM slow-wave sleep and REM sleep serve vital functions: NREM slow-wave sleep aids memory consolidation and physical repair, while REM sleep handles emotional processing through vivid dreams (3).

Sleep and Brain Injury

Following an acquired brain injury (ABI), whether caused by encephalitis, trauma, stroke, or another condition, sleep is often one of the first things to change. Studies suggest that the majority of people living with a brain injury experience some form of sleep disturbance, with more than 50 percent of children and more than 50 percent of adults with ABI experiencing sleep-wake disturbances in the months after hospital discharge (4, 5).

Some find it hard to fall asleep at all, lying awake as a racing or foggy mind refuses to switch off. Others drift off easily but wake repeatedly through the night, then cannot get back to sleep no matter how exhausted they feel. Vivid, intense, or unsettling dreams are also common, sometimes leaving people more drained than when they went to bed (6). Overwhelming daytime fatigue and the need to nap can blur the line between day and night, pushing the body's natural rhythms further out of step. Crucially, these changes are not a sign of weakness or of doing something wrong: they are a direct consequence of injury to the very organ that regulates sleep. Understanding this is the first step towards reclaiming rest.

Tips for improving sleep

To improve sleep after an ABI, there are several things one can do:

  • Get as much exposure to daylight as possible, while following sun safety advice (such as using sunscreen).
  • Engage in gentle activity during the day.
  • Avoid screens late at night or just before bed. They suppress melatonin, which helps regulate sleep.
  • Reduce caffeine and alcohol.
  • Consciously slow down nasal breathing (four to six breaths per minute if possible).
  • Keep a ‘sleep diary’ to share with your doctor.
  • Consider clinical sleep interventions such as CBT-I (cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia).
article continues after advertisement

The Role of Support Networks

Family members and caregivers play a crucial role in supporting healthy sleep during recovery. They can help maintain routines, create a restful environment, and advocate for appropriate medical interventions when needed. But they must also manage their own sleep and well-being too.

Furthermore, support groups, whether in-person or online through patient organisations, can provide practical strategies from others who've navigated similar challenges. Sometimes knowing you're not alone in your struggles makes them easier to bear.

A foundation for healing

Brain health, and particularly recovery from acquired brain injury (ABI), has its ups and downs. Prioritising sleep provides the foundation for recovery from this neurological condition.

The key is to take it one day at a time. If you are struggling with sleep during recovery, you are not alone. Speak with your medical team, connect with other people, and remember that sleep is one of the most important medicines for brain healing.

Prav Prathapan is Senior Medical Writer at Encephalitis International.

item.title: Your Brain Needs a Cognitive Immune System
item.description:
Cognition

Your Brain Needs a Cognitive Immune System

Five daily questions can train your mind to resist misinformation.

Posted July 27, 2026

Key points
  • The brain defaults to fast, intuitive thinking, which makes repeated and emotionally charged claims feel true.
  • Critical thinking taught as a one-time skill fades; practiced as a daily habit, it becomes automatic.
  • A five-question routine—the CIS-5—helps build "mental antibodies" against manipulation.
  • Intellectual humility, not blanket skepticism, is the goal.

You’ve felt it: the headline that lands like a punch, the statistic that confirms exactly what you suspected, the video that seems too outrageous not to share. Before you’ve consciously decided anything, your brain has already voted.

That vote is the problem. In an information environment shaped by algorithmic curation, emotionally optimized headlines, and AI-generated media that is increasingly indistinguishable from the real thing, the deepest threat isn’t misinformation itself. It’s cognitive autopilot—our tendency to accept whatever feels fluent, familiar, and emotionally resonant.

The good news: Just as the body builds immunity through repeated, low-dose exposure, the mind can build resistance to manipulation through small, daily acts of deliberate thinking. Call it a cognitive immune system.

Why Smart People Fall for Bad Information

Human cognition evolved for efficiency, not for epistemic vigilance. Decades of research on dual-process thinking show that we rely on fast, intuitive judgments unless something prompts us to slow down and engage effortful analysis (Kahneman, 2011). Slowing down is metabolically expensive, so the brain avoids it whenever it can.

Digital platforms exploit these defaults with precision. Consider the illusory truth effect: Simply repeating a claim makes it feel more accurate—even when people know better. In a series of experiments, Fazio and colleagues (2015) found that repetition increased belief in false statements even among participants who possessed the correct knowledge. Familiarity, it turns out, can quietly outvote facts.

Add time pressure, information overload, and emotionally activating content, and analytic thinking gets suppressed exactly when we need it most. Intelligence offers little protection here; the vulnerability is structural, not intellectual.

The Problem With How We Teach Critical Thinking

Most of us encountered critical thinking as a discrete lesson: a unit on logical fallacies, an essay on evaluating sources, a checklist consulted once and forgotten. These approaches are episodic. They treat critical thinking as a skill to be demonstrated rather than a function to be exercised.

But research on habit formation suggests that behaviors become automatic through frequent repetition in stable contexts—not through occasional intense effort (Lally et al., 2010). We rehearse epistemic theory in classrooms, then live in an environment that rewards epistemic shortcuts thousands of times a day. The shortcuts win.

The fix is not a better lecture on bias. It’s habit architecture.

The CIS-5: A Five-Minute Daily Protocol

The Cognitive Immune System protocol—CIS-5—is a structured, five-minute routine built around five questions. Applied to one claim per day, it targets the core mechanisms of sound reasoning: metacognitive monitoring, hypothesis generation, counterfactual thinking, and calibration.

article continues after advertisement

1. Friction: What claim did you encounter in the past 24 hours that felt immediately convincing or emotionally activating? (Immediacy and emotional charge are precisely the signals that intuition has already voted.)

2. Source trace: Where did this claim originate—and what incentives might shape that source? Follow it past the headline, past the share, to the primary material.

3. Alternative hypothesis: What is one plausible competing explanation? Generating even a single alternative disrupts the mind’s tendency to lock onto its first interpretation.

4. Evidence calibration: What kind of evidence would genuinely change your mind? If the honest answer is “nothing,” that’s diagnostic.

5. Confidence rating: On a scale of 0 to 100, how confident are you—and why? Putting a number on certainty forces the metacognitive check that autopilot skips.

Three design principles make this work. Frequency over intensity: Five minutes daily outperforms one high-stakes exercise. Metacognitive rehearsal: You practice noticing your own certainty, not just evaluating claims. Content independence: The protocol targets reasoning processes, so it applies equally to health claims, political news, financial advice, and viral videos.

What Changes With Practice

Over weeks, the questions start firing on their own. Practitioners report an intuitive “red flag” sensation when encountering unverified claims—cognitive friction that has itself become a habit. This mirrors findings from inoculation research, which shows that pre-emptive exposure to manipulation techniques measurably improves people’s ability to recognize them later (Roozenbeek et al., 2022).

article continues after advertisement

Tracking confidence ratings over time in a simple journal adds another benefit: improved calibration between how sure you feel and how right you are. That gap—overconfidence—is one of the most reliable findings in judgment research, and one of the few that responds to deliberate practice.

Perhaps most important, the protocol strengthens intellectual humility: the recognition that one’s beliefs might be wrong. Studies link intellectual humility to greater openness to opposing views and more accurate evaluation of evidence (Porter & Schumann, 2018). Changing your mind, in this framework, is not weakness. It is cognitive strength.

Calibrated Trust, Not Cynicism

A caution: The goal of a cognitive immune system is not skepticism toward everything. An immune system that attacks indiscriminately is a disorder, not a defense. Blanket cynicism is just autopilot in reverse—rejecting claims as reflexively as the credulous accept them.

The target is calibrated trust: confidence proportioned to evidence, held firmly enough to act on and loosely enough to revise.

In an era when algorithms amplify fluency and emotion, the most valuable thing you can amplify is friction and reflection. Five questions. Five minutes. Every day. That’s not a course in critical thinking—it’s a practice. And practice is what the moment demands.

This article was also published at Social Science Space.

item.title: Why Do Our Early Attachments Matter So Much?
item.description:
Attachment

Why Do Our Early Attachments Matter So Much?

Early attachments set the stage for future relationships, but that's not all.

Posted July 27, 2026

Key points
  • Protection and survival are not the only functions of early attachments.
  • Attachments shape our sense of self, of other people, and of the world.
  • Attachments have a central role in brain development and regulation of emotions.

The blueprints for our sense of who we are, our future relationships, and our development arise from a combination of our genetic givens and our experiences. The person or people to whom we are attached during our first few years (the caregiving environment) will have a major influence on how we develop.

The initial functions of the primary attachment bond are protection and survival, both of which depend on the presence of an adequate caregiver. John Bowlby, a British psychiatrist and psychoanalyst who studied young children separated from their parents during wartime, concluded that the caregiver relationship was as vital to mental health as nutrients were to physical health, and that attachment behaviors are biologically based (Bowlby, 1973). When infants feel stressed or threatened, the attachment system is activated, and they cry or signal the need for the caretaker in another way.

The second function of the attachment bond is the shaping of the sense of self, the sense of the other, and the expectations of how the world will respond to oneself. In early attachment relationships, the behaviors of each partner are shaping and being shaped by the other. Children’s attachment behaviors are intended to bring their caregivers closer to help them with their distress. How the caregiver behaves in response will influence how the child behaves in future moments of distress. In turn, the caregiving behaviors of the attachment figure will be influenced by the child’s behavior.

If the baby’s initial cries bring an immediate response and soothing, the baby learns to expect that, and develops a sense of confidence in the caregiver’s response and in themselves as worthy of care. Children begin to know that if they cry, the caregiver will be there. If there is no immediate response, attachment behaviors escalate—wailing, banging on the crib, flailing. If there is still no response, and this happens repeatedly, a baby may be unable to cope, falling into inconsolable states. In this situation, a sense of powerlessness, unworthiness, or despair can develop.

In the best situations, caregivers respond sensitively to the needs of the child, but infants and children develop attachment bonds with their primary caregivers even when their needs are not adequately met. When this happens, the attachments and self-concepts that arise will be more problematic. Early experiences of caring response or lack of care from a primary attachment figure can play an important part in future relationships by shaping expectations, instilling confidence or engendering doubt.

A third critical function of early attachment is its role in brain development. Certain regions of the brain are more experience-dependent and experience-susceptible for their development. For example, the orbito-frontal cortex, a key area for reasoning and associational processes, has a sensitive period for growth in the 6th to 12th month, dependent on exciting, pleasurable face-to-face interactions with the caregiver. States of positive arousal (like those in games of peek-a-boo) activate a rush of biological processes in which endorphins are released in the brain. Conversely, if the baby experiences prolonged states of negative arousal, as in being left alone to cry when hungry, stress hormones are released.

article continues after advertisement

The ability to moderate emotional arousal is present at birth but requires refinement and elaboration through interaction with a caregiver in order to develop. Affect regulation results from the interaction between the caregiver’s response to the baby’s affect and the baby’s central nervous system and neurotransmitter systems. When the infant is distressed, the stress response system is activated. If the caregiver responds in a timely way with soothing, arousal can diminish, and the infant can regain equilibrium in a more manageable environment. If the caregiver repeatedly fails to respond in a timely way or responds in a way that heightens negative arousal, the stress response system can be dysregulated in an ongoing way, interfering with the child’s ability to manage future stressful moments.

During the first year of life, the attachment relationship is the critical context in which development takes place. A sustained positive attachment can provide the learning of empathy, the control and balance of feelings, including destructive ones, and the optimal development of cognitive capacities. Patterns of soothing or lack of soothing—babies left alone to cry in states of arousal—are internalized at the body level (hormonally) and also representationally. Infants can perceive and store memory in ways that are later lost to us (Kaplow et al., 2006).

Attachment plays a crucial role in our early years, setting the stage for our future selves. Some of us face hurdles early on in life, made more challenging if our primary attachments have been disturbed or disrupted. Some of us are lucky enough to have a more promising beginning in life, giving us more capacity to deal with later challenges. Our brains and our emotions have plasticity, the capacity to change in response to new experiences, throughout life. Whatever our beginnings have been, subsequent positive attachment experiences in adolescence or adulthood have the potential to enable new patterns and responses.

item.title: The Fear System at Work
item.description:
Therapy

The Fear System at Work

How mutual distress can either hinder or deepen therapeutic connection.

Posted July 27, 2026

It was just the start of our second session, but we were in deep trouble already. Christopher was agitated, talking really quickly and with a sense of urgency. There was something he said I needed to know, but I couldn’t follow him; nothing made sense. The harder I tried, the more confused I got; I felt I was losing the plot. I thought: Is this a psychotic episode? That made me panic; my heart was beating fast, and I felt hot all over. What should I do? My mind went blank.

I thought, Here we go again, my fear system has just kicked off. I knew what to do now. Stop working, observe my breathing, nothing else. A couple of moments later, a bit calmer, I focused my attention on my body, my agitation and sense of disconnection, and my fear of craziness. A thought came into my head: “He’s scared he’s going mad.” At the same time, I had a mental picture of an astronaut, with his connection to his spacecraft severed, floating off into black, endless space.

We had a moment of real connection, then we were able to start working together to make sense of all of this, both of us having recovered the ability to think reflectively.

Right at the core of psychotherapy is the human fear system – a set of biological processes which form our instant, automatic and unconscious reactions to threat. We have three key fear responses depending on how close the danger is.

When the danger is some way off, and we are not sure what the threat is, we go into fear alert—our senses become more acute as we scan the environment, and our nervous system readies our body to explode into action if needed. We tense and hold our breath – we feel anxious, wary and on edge.

When danger is close, we are in fear arousal; the body changes and boosts our energy so we can hit harder and run faster to escape the threat. Where it is not obvious how to escape, our body might lock in a freeze or our heart rate might peak in terror, a state of ‘fright’ that can tip us into the final fear response. With fear arousal, we might experience a huge upwards-moving rush of energy such as when we really lose our temper—our heart beats faster—we run or shout or lash out, or we might go rigid in terror or panic and our mind blanks. In this state we can’t focus on anything but danger, and we lose our ability to think reflectively.

The third response is fear collapse, when the danger is so close there seems no escape from death, and a state of terror is combined with a feeling of being trapped. It involves a sudden drop in energy production throughout the body—a ‘sinking feeling’—the muscles lose all their tension and go limp, and much of the brain switches off. We can experience fear-collapse at different levels of intensity, ranging from low mood, depression, feeling wobbly and faint, brain-fog, or feeling useless and hopeless, to having sensations of being ‘out-of-body’ or unreal, extreme exhaustion, or ultimately physical collapse.

Our fear system can be life-saving—but it works optimally in short bursts, when there is a quick escape to a place of safety—the body calms and the fear system resets. When threat continues for too long, there is no safe place, no reset, and we get stuck in fear mode—a volatile fear-alert state. Every threat, serious or not, real or imagined, can trigger us into fear arousal or fear collapse. The longer we stay in this state, the harder it becomes for the fear system to reset, because the biological processes involved in this reset become impaired.

article continues after advertisement

The constant activation of our fear system has a disastrous impact on us. Over time, it can cause chronic fatigue, pain and physical illness, along with depression and anxiety. It leads to self-destructive behaviours, including addictions. It can destroy our ability to relate to others and our ability to think and learn. It can leave us in a state of misery. Being stuck in fear-mode over considerable periods of time is what we mean by ‘complex trauma’, and this is what all psychological therapists are working with every day.

Going back to Christopher, this was an example of the fear system at the core of the work of therapy. But, and this is important, it’s not just an issue for the client. Christopher’s acute state of fear arousal triggered my own fear arousal. I had to recognize and regulate this fear response in myself before I could be of any help to him. Once I’d done this, I could listen to what my fear response told me about Christopher’s state. This gave me an empathic understanding of what he was going through, which cut through his isolation and connected us. Being heard and understood brought him into a safe place, and that visceral sense of safety switched off his fear.

We don’t just find this in the therapy room. Whenever anyone in distress seeks our care, our own fear system can be triggered in response – we may feel inadequate or overwhelmed. If we can stop thinking there is something wrong with us when our fear is triggered and treat these sensations as information—an insight into how the other might be feeling—we can calm our own responses, thus offering the careseeker a place of safety and helping to draw them out of the misery of fear.

item.title: Your Brain Is Lying to You, On Purpose
item.description:
Positive Psychology

Your Brain Is Lying to You, On Purpose

How negativity bias built a survival system that's now sabotaging your peace.

Posted July 27, 2026

Our brains are powerful networks; they take in a lot of information. Even with the impressive processing power of the human brain, we can’t digest every single stimulus. To get anything done (including staying alive), we should have some system to filter out the noise. A way this happens is through what I call our interpretive lenses.

Interpretive lenses are just what they sound like: the things we look through to make sense of the world around us. The same way a pair of glasses affects how light hits your eyes and how you make sense of that information, these lenses help our brain interpret a situation, decide what’s important, and determine what course of action we should take. And as with the lenses in glasses, we rarely look at these interpretive lenses themselves. By nature, they’re invisible—they work without us ever thinking about them consciously, because their whole point is to make things more efficient for us. But they’re invisible, and it’s easy for us to forget (or never realize) we have them in the first place.

One of the lenses is the survival lens. Your brain’s main job is to keep you alive, and with that as priority one, ancient humans, as a matter of survival, focused more on stimuli that were dangerous or bad than on those that were safe or good. When the stakes were life-and-death, we needed a way to see and dwell on anything that could be a potential threat—one that we could deploy lightning-quick (and subconsciously). This is our survival lens, our way of interpreting the world so that we don’t get pulverized by it.

This lens, inherited from our Homo sapiens ancestors, works differently in a world where we’re not running from predators or worrying about which fruits are poisonous. In modern life, our survival lens means that the default setting in our mind is set to scrutinize all of our actions and other people’s behaviors instead of observing and learning from them; to make quick judgments rather than really considering whether a given stimulus represents the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth—displaying what you might know as a negativity bias.

But our survival lens isn’t just shaped only by the need to protect ourselves from predators. For humans, it’s not enough to stay alive (Am I safe?). We also want to live as individuals, to self-actualize, to have a real sense of self (Who am I?).

The ego is the part of the psyche that creates separation, individuality, and a sense of self. It says, “This is mine, and that is yours.” “Here’s where you end, and I start.” It is also working to help you survive—in this case, by ensuring your sense of place in the world as an individual. We often think of the ego as a bad thing, and considering that to “have an ego” is to be inherently full of yourself, but we all have an ego, and it’s part of how we exist as humans.

But here’s the thing about the ego: It loves to be right. If the ego could talk, its catchphrase would probably be “I told you so.” When it encounters any new information that challenges an existing belief, your ego says, “Whoa, wait a second!” It activates your fear response and subconsciously leads you to think that this new information must be wrong, dangerous, or otherwise untrustworthy. The truth is, the ego needs to be right to feel safe.

This means your survival lens is also fine-tuned for confirmation bias: to affirm what your ego already knows, and to push out anything that contradicts that “truth.” For example, if someone offers feedback or a different perspective, the unchecked ego interprets it as a threat—not an opportunity for growth because accepting that information might require rethinking something about yourself. On the other hand, your ego will always accept new information that confirms your beliefs. If you believe you’re not good at technology and you struggle with the new upgrade on your computer, this is confirmation. You’re not cut out for this. If you believe you’re underappreciated at work, your ego says, “I told you so,” when your boss gives praise to someone else at the meeting. These biases are often subconscious. However, they are what we carry with us by default unless we take the time to reflect and unpack them.

The bottom line is that these lenses aren’t good or bad or right or wrong—they just are. It’s what we do (or don’t do) with them that creates problems—usually because we don’t recognize that our truth isn’t the truth, and we don’t take the time to get curious about someone else’s lens.

By the same token, understanding that you have specific lenses that affect how you see things isn't about casting blame or beating up on yourself. It’s about cultivating an objective mindset so you can become a nonjudgmental observer and be curious about your thoughts, feelings, and actions, which is what reflection is all about. You don’t see the world as it is. You see the world as you are.

article continues after advertisement

There is so much beauty in that. As we start to realize that maybe the way I’m seeing it isn’t the way that everybody sees it, we also start to think, How can I shift my lens so that I can understand the way this other person might be seeing things? How could my lens be overfocusing on some parts of the story and not others? How could my lens be leaving out some things entirely? Once you get curious about these questions, it will lead you to the kind of growth that brings you closer to yourself, and closer to everyone around you.
